title: Words for the World
tagline: His printing press made knowledge cheap and revolutions possible.

scenes.text: Mainz, 1440s. Johannes Gutenberg works in secrecy — mixing wine-press mechanics with metalsmith's craft, experimenting with oil-based inks and hand-cast metal type.
The problem: copying a book takes a monk a year. Gutenberg's press can print 3,600 pages a day. The economics of knowledge are about to change forever.

challenge.fact: Gutenberg's breakthrough was casting individual metal letters that could be arranged, printed, and rearranged indefinitely. The same 26 letters (in his case Gothic type) could print any text in any order — unlike woodblocks, which could only print the single text carved into them. His oil-based ink and screw press were important innovations, but the movable metal type was the revolution.
challenge.instruction: What key innovation made Gutenberg's printing press transformative, compared to woodblock printing? Set the answer in movable type — mirrored, right to left.

scenes.text: He borrows heavily from a financier named Fust and pours everything into the Bible of 42 Lines — 180 copies, each identical, printed in two volumes.

challenge.fact: Gutenberg died nearly broke. His primary financial backer, Johann Fust, sued him over unpaid loans and won — seizing the printing equipment and the first run of Bibles. The press that changed the world made little money for its inventor. Gutenberg was awarded a pension by the Archbishop of Mainz in his final years, dying in 1468 largely unrewarded by the revolution he had started.
challenge.instruction: A note in a printer's grid code records how the inventor ended his days. Read it.

scenes.text: Fust sues him before the Bible is complete. Gutenberg loses the press and most copies. He dies relatively poor — but his invention has already escaped into the world.

challenge.fact: It took 50 years for printing to reach every corner of Europe. By 1500, over 20 million books had been printed — more than all the manuscripts produced in the previous thousand years of European history. The printing press did not merely copy existing knowledge; it transformed who could access it, who could challenge it, and who could add to it.
challenge.instruction: Arrange these consequences of Gutenberg's press in roughly chronological order after 1450: Gather what the story needs: match the goods until the tally is met.

scenes.text: Within 50 years, presses operate in every major European city. By 1500, 20 million books have been printed. The Reformation, the Scientific Revolution — impossible without Gutenberg.

challenge.instruction: Gutenberg's Mainz sat on the Rhine trade route linking the Hanseatic League's northern cities to Italy's wealth. Match the trading symbols as his Bibles flow out of the workshop and into a hungry Europe.
challenge.fact: The Hanseatic League — the great merchant confederation of northern Europe — had already built the infrastructure that carried Gutenberg's books. Trading cities like Lübeck, Hamburg, and Cologne had warehouses, ships, and agents throughout Europe, and they became the distribution network for the first mass-produced books. Commerce and knowledge traveled the same roads.

scenes.text: Gutenberg never became rich. But Time magazine named his press the most important invention of the second millennium. Every book, every newspaper, every democracy owes him a debt.

challenge.instruction: Gutenberg's press made Don Quixote possible — a book about a man who read too many books. Sort the scenes of the windmill chapter: without printing, this story could never have reached you.
challenge.fact: Cervantes' Don Quixote (1605) is sometimes called the first modern novel — and it exists because of Gutenberg. Without mass printing, literary culture remained in monasteries and palaces. With it, a middle-class Spaniard could read romances, go mad imagining himself a knight, and become a character in the world's first self-aware fiction.
